claim: The Japanese yen fell to about [160-163] yen per dollar in mid-2026, its lowest level against the US dollar in about 40 years [13:44].
quote: the yen is trading at about 160-ish yen per dollar, which is also the lowest level that it's been against the dollar in about 40 years
evidence: CNBC and CNN independently reported the yen weakening to roughly 162.8/$ in late June/early July 2026, its lowest level since 1986 -- a genuine ~40-year low, matching the video's figure and timeframe.

claim: Japan's 10-year government bond yield rose from about [0.25%] in 2022 to about [2.7%] by mid-2026, more than tenfold in four years [13:44].
quote: Today, it pays about 2.7%, which is more than 10 times higher in just 4 years
evidence: Japan's 10yr JGB traded near 0.25% under BOJ yield-curve-control in 2022 (tradingeconomics); by 10 Jul 2026 the yield stood at 2.760% per Reuters/Yahoo Finance coverage of the GPIF announcement. 2.76/0.25 = 11x, consistent with 'more than 10 times higher.' Arithmetic checks out on confirmed inputs.

claim: Japan's 30-year government bond yield was about [4%] around mid-2026 [13:44].
quote: The 30-year bond is at about 4%
evidence: Bloomberg reported Japan's 30-year JGB yield at 3.95% in July 2026 after surging to 4.2% in mid-May 2026 -- 'about 4%' sits within that range.

claim: Japan's government debt is over [200%] of GDP, the highest ratio of any developed country [03:13].
quote: Japan has more government debt relative to the size of its economy than any developed country in the world
evidence: Estimates put Japan's general government debt between roughly 199% and 237% of GDP depending on methodology, comfortably over 200% and the highest among developed/OECD economies in every ranking checked.

claim: The Bank of Japan holds about [48%] of all outstanding Japanese government bonds [04:17].
quote: The Bank of Japan itself holds about 48% of all Japanese government bonds
evidence: The BOJ's JGB share was about 46.3% at end-2024 and Nikkei Asia reported it dipping below 50% for the first time in 3.5 years in March 2026. 48% sits in the right range but the exact mid-2026 figure the video describes wasn't pinned to a precise date in the sources found, so this is capped at plausible.

claim: Japan's government bonds are held roughly [20%] by Japanese insurance companies, [14%] by Japanese banks, and less than [8%] by foreign investors [05:22].
quote: Japanese insurance companies hold another 20%, Japanese banks 14%, and the foreigners own less than 8%
evidence: MOF/BOJ flow-of-funds data reflected in these breakdowns puts insurance companies around 15.6% (not 20%) and banks around 14.5% (matches). Foreign holders were about 13.5% as of Dec 2023 -- well above the video's 'less than 8%.' The bank figure is accurate; the insurance figure is overstated and the foreign figure understated.

claim: Japan became the world's biggest foreign holder of US government debt, holding over [$1 trillion] of US Treasuries [06:26].
quote: Japan became the world's biggest foreign holder of US government debt
evidence: Japan overtook China as the top foreign holder of US Treasuries in 2019 and has remained in the top spot since, with holdings around $1.2 trillion as of December 2025 per Treasury TIC data reflected in these rankings -- comfortably 'over a trillion dollars.'

claim: On July 10, 2026, Japan's finance minister announced Japan wants its roughly [$1.8 trillion] GPIF pension fund to shift investments away from foreign assets and into Japanese assets [19:01].
quote: the Japanese government made an announcement about this. The finance minister of Japan said she wants the GPIF
evidence: Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on 10 July 2026 Japan wants to 'encourage pension funds, including GPIF, to make substantially greater investments in Japanese financial assets,' per wire coverage (Yahoo Finance/Reuters) and a widely circulated quote. GPIF held about $1.8 trillion in assets at the time, matching the video's figure.

claim: Japan's GPIF pension fund holds roughly [$230 billion] of US Treasuries plus hundreds of billions of dollars in US stocks [20:04].
quote: that fund holds roughly $230 billion of US Treasuries alone, plus hundreds of billions of dollars in US stocks
evidence: A Reuters factbox reports GPIF holds $931 billion in foreign assets, including $232.1 billion in US Treasuries -- matching 'roughly $230 billion' almost exactly. The remaining foreign-asset pool includes equities in the hundreds-of-billions range, consistent with 'hundreds of billions... in US stocks.'

claim: Japan's Ministry of Finance spent [$73 billion] in April and May 2026 buying yen to defend the currency [16:55].
quote: In April and May, Japan's Ministry of Finance spent 73 billion dollars buying their own currency, the yen
evidence: CNBC reported Japanese authorities spent a record ~$73.5 billion (11.7 trillion yen) in April and May 2026 defending the yen -- matching the video's figure almost exactly.

claim: The April-May 2026 yen intervention only worked for about [3 weeks] before the yen fell again, and the Bank of Japan's subsequent June 2026 rate hike to [1%] -- the highest level since 1995 -- also failed to stop the decline [17:57].
quote: in June, the Bank of Japan increased rates to 1% and the yen went down anyway
evidence: The same CNBC report confirms the BOJ 'recently raised its benchmark interest rate to 1%, the highest level in more than three decades' -- i.e. since 1995 or earlier -- and that the yen kept weakening despite both the FX intervention and the rate hike.

claim: The 10-year US Treasury yield was about [4.7%] in mid-2026, which the video calls 'close to all-time highs' [22:09].
quote: it's paying about 4.7%, which is close to all-time highs
evidence: The 10-year Treasury's all-time high is about 15.84% (September 1981) -- more than three times the ~4.7-4.8% level in mid/late-2026, which is only near a post-2007 high (highest since October 2023). 'Close to all-time highs' is a clear factual error, not a rounding issue.

claim: On July [20th], 2026, Japan passed a law -- described as Japan's version of the US CLARITY Act -- recognizing crypto as a financial asset and cutting the tax on Japanese crypto gains from [55%] to [20%] [23:11].
quote: Japan passed something that's being called their version of America's Clarity Act
evidence: Japan's parliament passed the reclassification amendments on July 15, 2026 (Coindesk, citing Reuters/NHK) -- not July 20. The substance is accurate: crypto is reclassified as a financial asset and gains will be taxed at a flat 20%, down from a top rate of 55%, and 'Reverse CLARITY Act' framing does appear in real coverage. Kernel of truth on substance; the specific date is off by five days.

claim: Article 589 of Japan's Civil Code establishes that a lender cannot charge interest on a loan unless interest was expressly agreed [23:11].
quote: Article 589 basically says a lender cannot charge interest on a loan unless the interest was agreed to
evidence: Article 589 (Section 5, Loans for Consumption) of Japan's 1896 Civil Code is an ordinary default rule: interest is not owed on a loan unless the parties agreed to it. Independent analyses of the viral claims confirm this plain description of the statute is accurate.

claim: Article 589 gives Japan 'a little more control over where their money's going' and is 'one way they're forcing the wealth back home,' letting Japan block foreign borrowers from continuing to refinance cheap yen loans [23:11].
quote: which essentially allows Japan to have a little more control over where their money's going
evidence: Independent analysis of the viral Article 589 claims concludes the statute 'does not govern bank lending decisions, cross-border funding, loan roll-overs, or capital flows,' and that 'Japanese banks do not invoke Article 589 to cut off foreign borrowers or force mass repayments' -- it is an 1896 default rule for private consumption loans, applied by courts in ordinary domestic interest disputes. There is no mechanism giving the Japanese government leverage over foreign borrowers or capital repatriation through it.

claim: Japan's new crypto financial-asset law will allow Japanese stablecoins to be backed by Japan's own government bonds, giving Japan a buyer for its debt [24:15].
quote: this will allow Japan's stablecoins to be backed by their own government bonds
evidence: Coverage of the July 2026 law describes it as reclassifying crypto assets (Bitcoin, XRP, etc.) under the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act; stablecoins are described as regulated separately under payment-services rules, a different legal track, with foreign-issued stablecoin rules finalized in May 2026. No source found ties this specific reclassification law to a JGB-backed domestic stablecoin scheme -- searched three angles without locating the mechanism the video describes.

claim: Tether is the biggest corporate owner of US Treasuries [24:15].
quote: It's a company that is the biggest corporate owner of US Treasuries
evidence: Trade press reports Tether as the 17th-largest holder of US Treasuries overall and the top non-sovereign/corporate holder, with about $141 billion in exposure as of Q1 2026 -- but every figure ultimately traces back to Tether's own quarterly attestation report (a source about itself), so this is capped at plausible rather than confirmed regardless of media pickup.

claim: In August 2024, the Bank of Japan raised interest rates by a quarter of one percent, the yen rose, and in one day Japan's stock market fell about [12%] -- the worst day since 1987 -- while the US stock market fell about [3%] [27:26].
quote: in one day Japan's stock market went down 12%. The worst day since 1987 and the US stock market went down 3%
evidence: The Nikkei 225 fell 12.4% on August 5, 2024 -- its worst day since the 1987 Black Monday crash -- following the BOJ's late-July rate hike from near-zero to 0.25%; the S&P 500 fell 3% the same day. Matches the video's figures closely.

claim: An anonymous X account posting under the persona of a Bank of Japan insider ('Yuto') published a post reading, in part, 'To the people of the Western countries, I offer my deepest apologies,' which the video says got millions of views [00:00].
quote: The measures being prepared by the Bank of Japan will affect the lives of billions of people. To the people of the Western countries, I offer my deepest apologies. This is not a personal matter. May God's blessings be upon you.
evidence: The exact wording of the quoted post is corroborated word-for-word and the account (@yutokanzakireal) is real. But it is pseudonymous, its own bio reads 'It's all a lie,' and there is no official confirmation from the Bank of Japan behind it -- the video itself hedges appropriately ('no one really knows who this person is'). The specific 'millions of views' figure was not independently confirmed.

claim: At the peak of Japan's 1980s bubble economy, the land under the Imperial Palace in Tokyo was worth more than all the real estate in California [03:13].
quote: the land under the Imperial Palace in Tokyo was worth more than all the real estate in California
evidence: A widely repeated factoid from Japan's 1980s asset bubble, retold across multiple retrospectives (SCMP among them); the underlying valuation likely traces to a single period estimate rather than independent recalculations, so this reads as a judged, single-origin figure rather than something independently re-measured.

claim: Japan's debt-to-GDP ratio (over 200%) is higher than Greece's was when Greece's debt crisis hit [03:13].
quote: that means Japan has more debt than Greece when Greece collapsed
evidence: Greece's debt-to-GDP ratio was roughly 130% in 2009, rising to about 180% by 2014 -- both well below Japan's 200%+.

claim: Japan has more government debt relative to GDP than any country that has ever experienced hyperinflation [03:13].
quote: They have more debt than any country that's ever hyper-inflated
evidence: Checked against the two most commonly cited hyperinflation cases: Weimar Germany's debt-to-GDP was about 131% before its 1923 hyperinflation (which then eroded the ratio toward zero); Zimbabwe's external public debt reached roughly 119-166% of GDP at its 2008 peak. Both are below Japan's 200%+, but this is a broad 'any country ever' claim not exhaustively checked against every historical hyperinflation episode, so it stays plausible rather than confirmed.

claim: Japan experienced roughly three decades of deflation following the early-1990s bubble collapse [04:17].
quote: Japan went into something that no modern economy had ever experienced. Which was three decades of deflation
evidence: Japan's prices were largely stagnant or falling from the mid-1990s through the early 2020s -- commonly described as Japan's 'lost decades' -- though the period is more accurately near-zero/deflationary than continuously falling every single year.

claim: The Bank of Japan kept interest rates at essentially zero for about 30 years [04:17].
quote: the Bank of Japan lowered interest rates to zero, and basically left them there for 30 years
evidence: BOJ ultra-low/zero rates ran, with brief interruptions (a short hike to 0.25% in Aug 2000 was reversed by March 2001), from Feb 1999 through March 19, 2024, when the BOJ ended negative rates and yield curve control -- 'the bank rate had not been raised for 17 years.' 'Basically zero for 30 years' fairly rounds a ~25-year near-zero-rate era but glosses over the brief normalization attempts.

claim: Since 2004, the US money supply (M2) grew by about [280%], Canada's grew by about [370%], while Japan's grew by only about [90%] [05:22].
quote: Since 2004, the US money supply grew by about 280% Canada grew by 370% but Japan only grew by 90
evidence: One analysis puts Canada's M2 growth since March 2004 at 362% versus 270% for the US, with Japan's growth well under a quarter of Canada's (consistent with ~90%) -- within a few points of the video's numbers, but drawn from a single financial-blog analysis rather than a primary central-bank comparison.

claim: The yen carry trade is estimated to be worth trillions of dollars of investment globally [06:26].
quote: That's estimated to be worth trillions of dollars of investments all around the world
evidence: Estimates of the yen carry trade's size vary hugely by methodology, from roughly $880 billion (a narrow BIS-based measure) to $4-20 trillion under broader measures. 'Trillions of dollars' is defensible under most of the wider estimates but not the narrowest one.

claim: By 2022, Japan recorded 2% inflation for the first time in decades [08:29].
quote: By 2022, Japan got 2% inflation for the first time in decades
evidence: Japan's inflation sustainably crossed the BOJ's 2% target from around April 2022 for the first time in decades of near-zero/deflationary readings, averaging about 2.5% for the year and peaking above 4% in Dec 2022-Jan 2023.

claim: The US raised interest rates to about [5%] [09:33].
quote: the US raised interest rates to 5%
evidence: The Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate to a range of 5.25%-5.50% by July 2023, its highest level since 2001 -- 'raised to 5%' is a fair round figure.

claim: The yen weakened from around [110] per dollar to [150], then [160] [09:33].
quote: the strength of the yen collapses from around 110 per dollar to 150, then 160
evidence: USD/JPY moved from roughly 115 in early 2022 through the 150s in 2023 and past 160 by 2024-2026, consistent with the independently confirmed 40-year-low reporting in claim 1.

claim: Japan imports almost all of its energy, and that energy is priced in dollars [10:35].
quote: they don't make their own oil
evidence: Japan imports 97-99.7% of its oil, LNG and coal, and net imports made up about 90% of Japan's total energy supply in 2022, per Japan's own energy agency (METI) and Statista -- 'almost all' checks out; oil is conventionally priced in dollars globally.

claim: Japanese workers got the biggest pay raises in over three decades [11:38].
quote: they got the biggest pay raises in over three decades
evidence: Bloomberg: Japan's 2024 shunto wage negotiations concluded with a 5.1% average pay gain, the most in 33 years.

claim: In the week before the video was made, Japan's inflation came in at [1.6%], below the Bank of Japan's 2% goal, for the fifth month in a row, while on the same day Japan's stock market fell over [2%] and about [30 trillion yen] was lost [14:50].
quote: inflation came in at 1.6%
evidence: Japan's core inflation did undershoot the 2% target repeatedly in 2026 with a reading of 1.6% (June), but independent counts of the consecutive-month streak vary (one report cites a seventh straight month, not fifth), and no independent report was found tying a specific >2% stock-market drop and ~30 trillion yen loss to that same release date -- searched but couldn't pin the exact day or reconcile the month count.

claim: Last time the yen was this weak against the dollar, Ronald Reagan was US president and Nintendo had just come out [13:44].
quote: the last time this was happening, Ronald Reagan was president and Nintendo had just come out
evidence: The yen's prior comparable low was 1986 (CNBC: lowest level 'since 1986'); Reagan was US president 1981-1989, and Nintendo's Famicom/NES launched in Japan in 1983 and the US in 1985 -- both true of 1986.

claim: Banks including JPMorgan have suggested [164] yen per dollar as a 'line in the sand' beyond which Japan would intervene [13:44].
quote: Banks like JP Morgan are saying that 164 yen per dollar is kind of like the magic line in the sand
evidence: FX analysts from various banks floated a range of 'line in the sand' intervention levels through 2026 (160, 162, 163, 165 among them) and JPMorgan strategists commented on intervention triggers generally, but no source found specifically attributes the number 164 to JPMorgan. The general concept is well documented; the specific attribution is not confirmed.

claim: Hedge funds' net short position against the yen reached about [-150,000] futures contracts, worth roughly [$11-12 billion] [15:51-16:55].
quote: This is around -150,000 contracts
evidence: CFTC data showed leveraged-fund net short yen positions near 138,000 contracts at end-June 2026, the largest since 2007 (a 19-year high) -- close to the video's ~150,000 figure. At roughly $80-90k notional per contract near 150-160 yen/$, that scale is consistent with an $11-12bn-plus notional estimate.

claim: Japan still has enough foreign-exchange reserves for about 15 more interventions of the [$73 billion] size used in April-May 2026 [17:57].
quote: Japan still has enough money for 15 more interventions of this size
evidence: Japan's official reserve assets totaled about $1.29 trillion at end-July 2026. $73 billion x 15 = about $1.1 trillion, close to the full reserve stock -- a directionally reasonable back-of-envelope estimate, though it would mean spending nearly all reserves, not leaving a comfortable cushion.

claim: Bloomberg data shows Japanese life and casualty insurance companies swung from selling to being the biggest net buyers of long-term Japanese government bonds in three years [20:04-21:07].
quote: The last bar shows the biggest buying in 3 years
evidence: Bloomberg reported Japanese life and casualty insurers bought a net ~630.5 billion yen (~$3.9bn) of bonds with maturities over a decade in June 2026 -- the most since July 2023, roughly three years.

claim: Japan is building its first centralized intelligence agency since World War II [22:09].
quote: Japan wants to build its own intelligence agency for the first time since World War II
evidence: CNN and Al Jazeera both independently confirm Japan's Diet passed legislation in mid-2026 to establish its first centralized intelligence agency since WWII, motivated by threats from Russia, China and North Korea -- unrelated to yen/bond dynamics, but the underlying fact is accurate.

claim: SoFi is the first nationally chartered retail bank where customers can buy, sell, and hold over 25 cryptocurrencies [07:27].
quote: they're the first national chartered bank where retail customers can buy, sell, and hold over 25 cryptocurrencies
evidence: Multiple outlets reported SoFi's 'first nationally chartered bank' crypto-trading claim, but all trace back to SoFi's own press release about itself -- a claim about a company by the company is capped at tier 4/plausible regardless of media pickup. Appears in the video as a disclosed, paid sponsor read.

claim: In 1998, during the collapse of the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management, the yen rose about [15%] in just three days [26:21].
quote: In 1998, the yen went up 15% in just 3 days
evidence: The Bank of England's own analysis records the yen appreciating 14% over 6-8 October 1998 (other sources cite up to 17% over 48 hours) amid the LTCM unwind -- the video's '15% in 3 days' sits squarely within the documented range.

claim: In 2011, the yen hit a record high against the dollar [26:21].
quote: 2011, record yen high, peak global fear
evidence: The yen hit an all-time high of about 76.25/$ in March 2011 (later 75.58 in October 2011), confirmed by contemporaneous CNBC reporting.

claim: During the 2008 financial crisis, the yen rose for the whole year as the carry trade unwound [26:21].
quote: in 2008, the yen goes higher all year long
evidence: USD/JPY fell from about 110 to 76 (a 25%+ yen appreciation) over roughly six months around the 2008 crisis as carry trades unwound -- a real and large move, though 'all year long' overstates the duration somewhat versus the documented ~6-month window.

claim: An unnamed economist compared Japan's simultaneous currency intervention and rate hikes to 'tapping the brakes while keeping your other foot on the gas' [17:57].
quote: tapping the brakes while keeping your other foot on the gas
evidence: Rhetorical framing attributed only to 'one economist,' with no name given -- an analogy, not a checkable factual assertion.
